title: Vaisakhi with family
hookLine: the Khalsa's birthday lived at home and in the procession
tomorrow: why would a whole sangat sing in the street before sunrise?

lines: A KURTA ON THE KITCHEN COUNTER.
cards: It's barely light and the house is already loud. Someone is ironing a kurta on the kitchen counter. An uncle is on speakerphone from another time zone, asking if the parade has started.
A pot of kheer is cooling on the stove, and nobody is allowed to touch it yet. Out at the curb, a flatbed truck washed the night before sits waiting to carry the Guru through town.
Whose birthday turns a whole street into family? Not one person's. A people's.

teach.h: THE HARVEST DAY, THE KHALSA'S BIRTHDAY.
teach.b: It's Vaisakhi, the spring harvest day, and Sikhs keep it as the Khalsa's birthday.

Tradition says that on a Vaisakhi at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh asked the gathered sangat who would give their head for the Guru, and the ones who rose became the Panj Pyare, the beloved five, the first of the Khalsa.
Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight.

teach.h: A FATHER, A MOTHER, A HOME.
teach.b: In the amrit ceremony, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada lays it out, a new Khalsa Sikh is told who their family now is: Guru Gobind Singh their father, Mata Sahib Kaur their mother, Anandpur their home.
So the Khalsa's birthday is, quite literally, a family birthday. That's why it gets lived in two places at once.

teach.h: IN THE STREET AND AT THE TABLE.
teach.b: In the street: the nagar kirtan, the Guru Granth Sahib carried in a palki, the sangat singing behind it, langar on the sidewalk for anyone.

And at home: an early gurdwara visit, new clothes, something sweet, calls to relatives far away. Some families close the day with the Anand Sahib, Guru Amar Das's song of bliss, the hymn sung as a gathering ends.
It opens with a family word: anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa.

teach.h: BLISS HAS COME, O MY MOTHER.
teach.b: Bliss has come, O my mother: I have found the True Guru.
A birthday, a mother, a home found.

how: Sikhs mark Vaisakhi as the Khalsa's birthday with a gurdwara visit, kirtan, Ardas and langar, and in some towns a nagar kirtan; at home families share something sweet, new clothes and calls to relatives.

o: the day new Sikhs take amrit with their parents
keeping the Khalsa's birthday at home and in the street
a harvest meal for relatives, with no religious side

games.q: the Khalsa's birthday — tap the pairs.
p: the harvest day, the Khalsa's birthday
the beloved five who rose first
bliss has come, O my mother

s: Vaisakhi is only a harvest festival, with no Sikh meaning
Sikhs keep it as the Khalsa's birthday, from the call at Anandpur.
at amrit, a new Khalsa Sikh is told that Anandpur is their home
the Rehat Maryada names a father, a mother and a home: a family.
the celebration belongs only inside the gurdwara
it's lived in the street too: the nagar kirtan, and langar on the sidewalk for anyone.

games.q: your aunt works a night shift on Vaisakhi and can't make the gurdwara or the parade. she says the day is lost this year. what fits the lesson?
o: the day is still hers: something sweet, a call home, the Anand at the table.
she should swap shifts; the day only counts at the procession itself.
skip it this year; Vaisakhi is mainly for people taking amrit.
games.why: Vaisakhi is lived in two places, the street and the home. a family birthday can be kept at a kitchen table, after a night shift too.

practice: Bring to mind one person you'd want beside you on a day like this, near or far. See where you'd be together and what's on the table, then name what might get in the way: distance, a shift, an old argument.
Choose one small, real step that would bring you closer, and hold it there for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Vaisakhi with family. The Khalsa's birthday, kept in the street and at the kitchen table, by a people given one father, one mother and one home.

orig.note: Punjabi: the day that opens the month of Vaisakh, kept by Sikhs as the Khalsa's birthday.

carryVoice: Keep this one: vaisakhi together, because a birthday was never meant to be kept alone. Day 1751, and the kheer is finally open.
